feed.title: Today's Darling
feed.subtitle: Daily essays by Shigesato Itoi from 1101.com, translated to English.

entry.title: Do you like "like"?
entry.content:
A film about somebody loving somebody else tends to leave you feeling good. Ah, but maybe that's not always true. It isn't always true, and yet, more often than not, surprisingly, it turns out to be a fine thing.

Not just love stories, either. The feeling you have for a friend, for the people around you. A gentle tenderness toward small things. A liking that's almost like longing. A liking you never quite realize is liking.

In the reality of living, what does a person actually do for the one they care about? What form does that feeling take? These are things we rarely get to see. Now and then we catch a glimpse, sure.

When you've come to like someone, how do you feel? What do you find yourself wanting to do? You put that feeling out into the open, then pull it back in again. The only records of such things exist in two places: inside stories, and inside yourself.

How do people who like each other behave? While we watch it unfold in a story, we find ourselves remembering our own feelings of liking. Not just love stories, but anywhere that liking is expressed, it comes back to us.

That we exist, and that within us there is this thing called liking. It would be good to have many chances to remember that. A world where dislike is easier to find than liking is not a particularly happy one to live in.

◆Now then, question no.024 is: "On your twentieth birthday?" Where were you, who were you with, what were you thinking? If you feel like it, write it in an email and send it my way.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. If you never let yourself like anything, life would be easier. Is that so, though?
entry.summary: Films about love and human connection remind us of our own capacity to care for others, and in a world where dislike comes more easily than affection, cultivating and recognizing these feelings of liking—whether romantic or tender—becomes essential to living a meaningful life.

entry.title: What it means to have "baka" attached
entry.content:
"That Itoi, he's a good-natured fool, honest to the point of stupidity." The one they were saying this about wasn't me, it was my father. He'd often sit drinking and talking with his close friends. That phrase, "good-natured to the point of stupidity," was, in its way, a bit of affectionate name-calling among people who liked each other. They'd even say things like, "He's a fool, a fool, a great big fool." And my father, on the receiving end, didn't seem to mind at all. If anything, he sat there grinning, thoroughly pleased with himself. Even then, I could sense it was a kind of backhanded praise.

Maybe the reason I remember it all so vividly is that the same scene played out over and over, again and again. To me as a child, though, the word "fool" seemed to be getting thrown around a little too conveniently, and I have to admit it wasn't a conversation I enjoyed.

Good-natured to the point of being a fool, honest to the point of being a fool. In a certain sense, isn't that an "invincible" banner to wave? A banner that cancels out all sorts of other, less flattering qualities. If it were me today, I might well have cut in with, "Come on, nobody's actually like that."

Later, once I was no longer a child, a manga called "Karate Baka Ichidai" ran in serialization, and, well, I read it avidly. But the way "fool" is used there is a little sly too, isn't it? If everyone else is "not a fool," then this particular "fool" starts to look like something good, something worth protecting. And I believe it was Fujio Akatsuka who came up with it, but Yuya Uchida's nickname, "the rock 'n' roll fool," has that same effect of neutralizing everything else about a person.

"Fool," as long as you're the one claiming it for yourself, is probably a wonderfully convenient word, like a crown you place on your own head. And that's precisely because it's a word you'd hate to have aimed at you. He who willingly dons the "crown of the fool" shall be revered. Not that I have any intention of going and doing that myself.

◆Now then, question no. 023 is: "Do you drink?" I wonder what sort of stories will begin once that question is asked. If you'd like, do write in and send us an email.

Thank you, as always, for stopping by Hobonichi today. Come to think of it, there are drinking scenes in "Chiikawa" too, aren't there.
entry.summary: The essay explores how calling someone a "fool"—when done affectionately and especially when self-claimed—becomes a disarming compliment that neutralizes criticism and creates an almost invincible social position. The author reflects on witnessing his father receive such backhanded praise and considers how this paradoxical label works as a convenient shield in human relationships.

entry.title: This short piece was "Today's Darling."
entry.content:
This piece I write every day was originally called "Today's Darling." The joke was in getting people to go out of their way to call someone like me "Darling." I mean, "It doesn't suit me at all, does it? Heh heh heh." But little by little it stuck, and time went on, and new people kept arriving, until eventually we reached an age of "What's a Darling?" So I've been quietly trying to retire the name.

After all, the recent newcomers to Hobonichi didn't even know who Led Zeppelin was. They'd say things like, "I gave them a listen, and they're actually pretty good." Soon enough, everyone will be someone who's never heard of Shigesato Itoi either, and "What's this Darling business?" will be the natural order of things. So we've got to keep changing things up.

Which is why this daily piece I'm writing right now doesn't have a settled name. When I send in the manuscript, I, the person actually writing it, still just tentatively file it under "Today's Darling."

The feeling that I need to change is something I carry with me always. And yet I'm also the kind of guy who wants to keep feeling, always, the texture of the things that don't change.

So we started this daily series, remember, where we interview readers with the invitation, "Write to us by email if you'd like." Reading these every day is genuinely one of my great pleasures. There really are all sorts of people out there. Some of them answer like it's a survey, just a curt "Yes" and nothing more, but that too is part of "everyone." It really makes you feel, deeply, that each person has their own "LIFE."

The stories about fathers and mothers especially, the love and the hatred and everything in between, they were something to read. It's astonishing, the "connection" that runs between parent and child. Sometimes envious, sometimes silently applauding in my heart, I've been reading through so many of them, as the interviewer.

As an aside, the characters in "Chiikawa," every one of them, they're solitary beings with no family. Small, cute, and standing on their own two feet. That too gets to me, right in the chest.

◆Now then, today's a big one. No. 022, "How are you doing?" Ask yourself again, really. And if you feel like it, write to me by email and let me read your answer.

Thank you again for coming to Hobonichi today. Around the office right now, with the release of the Hobonichi Techo coming up, everyone's in a wonderful, spinning frenzy.
entry.summary: The author reflects on embracing change while honoring what remains constant, finding deep meaning in the everyday connections and individual stories shared by readers who participate in the daily series.

entry.title: I haven't given up on my "Chiikawa calligraphy"
entry.content:
I've never been any good at lessons, the kind you practice at. I've given up on so many of them over the years. I don't know why exactly, but they genuinely wear me down. Memorizing the steps, the lines, the choreography, I just can't do it. When I was young I thought this was something I ought to overcome, but now I'm thoroughly grown up, and once I started doing things as part of a team, we realized it was better to divide the work by what each person was good at rather than forcing yourself through what you weren't. So I threw myself into the things I was good at, and left the things I struggled with to other people.

I assumed I'd just keep going that way. But lately I've been earnestly doing the very thing I was always bad at. It's called rinsho: you look at a model and reproduce the flow of the brush. It's a practice repeated endlessly in the world of calligraphy. The other day I started my own version, "Chiikawa rinsho." I copy the characters that the creator, Nagano-san, draws.

With what motion of the brush, in what shape, in what position, at what size is this little one drawn? When I move my hand trying to draw it the same way, little by little, some things start to come clear. And if I can get the technique into my hands, I should be able to draw something close to a real "Chiikawa."

The original manga is drawn by hand by Nagano-sensei, but so much of it has been adapted into animation as secondary work that there must be some "rule" governing these shapes made of lines and dots. The animators have mastered it, which is how they can both reproduce the original art and make it move. In a sense it's different from the original drawings, and yet within the range that satisfies the viewer, it is more than sufficiently "Chiikawa."

I don't need to get all that good at it. But I'd love to draw a "Chiikawa" that seems to have just welled up onto the sketchbook page on its own. I hope I can get that far. I do a little rinsho every day, but the road looks long.

◆ And now, question no. 021: "Have you ever had a fight with someone?" Think back, and if you feel like it, write it up in an email and send it over.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. The things that look like anyone could do them are exactly the ones that turn out to be so hard.
entry.summary: The author discovers that by practicing calligraphy through patient, daily imitation of a beloved character's style, they're finally embracing the very kind of disciplined learning they once avoided—finding that mastering fundamentals, no matter how tedious, can unlock genuine creative ability.

entry.title: On August 24th, a day that seems like nothing special.
entry.content:
Recently, I wrote a rather definitive line: "When you feel the first signs of autumn, that's summer fatigue setting in."

I've felt this way since about two years ago. When you notice things like "the wind has turned cooler" or "the cicadas are singing differently," that means autumn is on its way, right? I think I've got that part correct. And it's right around when you feel those things that "your body starts acting strange."

In the dead of summer, when I was constantly going on about how hot it was, I could blame everything on the heat, so I never noticed. But all those days of it pile up as fatigue in the body. And then, once things cool down even a little, that's when you realize, "Ah, I'm exhausted." That's how I've come to think of it.

You know how when you're out running you don't sweat while you're moving, but the moment you stop, you're suddenly drenched? I feel like it's something like that.

But I have no idea whether any of this is actually true. It's really nothing more than my own personal "explanation of summer fatigue." For that matter, I don't even really understand the concept of "summer fatigue" itself. Do people get worn out at the end of summer, in every country? Until a few years ago, I didn't even know what "summer fatigue" was.

(In moments like this, if you just ask an AI, the answer comes right up. Let's see now, oh, I see, ah, that does make sense...)

...Summer fatigue is a real thing. And it seems my own sense of it wasn't far off, either. In summer, the body works hard to cope with the heat. Regulating body temperature, the strain on the autonomic nervous system, fluid balance, lack of sleep, all of it, the body wears itself out adapting to the heat. And then, just as you've finally gotten a body suited to the heat, the "autumn wind" starts to blow. Of course you end up thinking, "Oh, come on, really?" Absolutely.

So it comes back to that opening line, "When you feel the first signs of autumn, that's summer fatigue setting in." That's it. And I've definitely got summer fatigue.

◆Today's question, no.020: "What was your mother like?" It's been ten days since no.010, so take a moment to remember. If you'd like, write it down and send it to us by email.

Thank you for coming to Hobonichi again today. Summer really is coming to an end, isn't it, all you children on summer break.
entry.summary: The author describes summer fatigue as the accumulated exhaustion from the body's constant effort to regulate heat throughout summer, which only becomes noticeable when autumn's cooler temperatures arrive and the physical strain finally ceases. This personal observation about delayed awareness of exhaustion reflects a universal physiological reality that the author validates through research.

entry.title: On prose and the act of writing
entry.content:
Specifications, instruction manuals, work memos, the so-called "practical texts" of the world, all aim to convey what needs conveying as accurately as possible. "September 1st (Tuesday) is finally the release date for the Hobonichi Techo 2027," that sort of thing belongs to this category. If anything, that one word, "finally," carries just a little bit of "the feelings of the person who wrote it."

Not everything written in the world is a practical text. There are things that hold the "self" of the writer. You don't need to strike a grand pose and call it "literature." Just as most ordinary chatter does, it's simply something a person wants to say, expressed toward another person. Even "Man, I'm sad" is a form of self-expression.

"I want everyone in the world to understand" is impossible. But then again, "it's fine if only the people who get it get it" won't do either.

Being understood is a bit like a prize, and as you keep winning prizes, your writing gets better. But then, that leads to a new problem, because you start writing with the prize in mind. Honestly, I suspect the best thing would be to stop worrying about it, about understanding or being understood.

To put it very crudely, writing can be divided into two kinds: the "instruction manual" and the "song." Every piece of writing is a blend of the two. What I'm writing right now is one such blend, and this thing I've been going on about lately, "subjectivity," belongs to the "song" side of things. Take it away, and everything turns into nothing but instruction manuals.

◆ The daily interviews. I read tons of them every day, you know. So today, here's this one. No. 019, "Where were you born?" It's a question I have no memory of myself, but how about it? If you'd like, write it in an email and send it my way.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. The times we're born and the times we die, those are the things we ourselves never get to know.
entry.summary: Writing exists on a spectrum between purely practical communication and personal self-expression ("instruction manual" versus "song"), and the most meaningful writing balances both rather than obsessing over whether others will understand it.

entry.title: Thinking about things that don't become new.
entry.content:
People love to say things like, "This is how the times are now." The media says it, and so do the people who fancy themselves ahead of the curve. As for me, I'm apparently seen as someone fond of novelty, and I sometimes get asked for my opinions on such things.

But it's nothing to brag about, and the truth is, I'm not the least bit new. I'm not one of those people who clings to old ways and calls it "having standards," but honestly, I keep a pretty careful distance from anything new.

The same goes for how I work. I'm not doing anything new there either. Every time some theory becomes the topic of the day, some "such-and-such organization" or "so-and-so management style," I get asked in interviews, "Hobonichi is one of those such-and-such organizations, isn't it?" And I'm left at a loss, because I've honestly never really thought about it. I might scramble to read a book or two on the subject after the fact, but since I never built my work around any theory to begin with, even when something strikes me as insightful, that's all it amounts to.

Whenever there's a theory or a principle, and the idea is to work toward it, I can't help feeling it tends to lock you into a mold. Having a clear mold is convenient for streamlining things, for smoothing everything out, but getting drawn into that kind of competition just isn't our strength.

Still, whether things are new or old, whatever the era may be, I think there are things that stay the same no matter what. Like, people way back in ancient times wouldn't have liked being treated this way either. Or, if someone did this for you, wouldn't that make you happy. Or, anyone would fall for a thing like this.

These are the "feelings of the heart" that exist within me and within everyone else. Throughout the long history of humankind, they've never changed, and in the times ahead, they'll seem to change and yet stay the same.

As for what exactly those unchanging things are, I do think we should keep considering it seriously, sparing no effort. The people of old spoke of "learning the new by studying the old," and it's no different today.

◆ no.018: "If you were to compare yourself to another living creature, what would it be?" Give it some thought. It might be fun to read them all together someday. If you feel like it, write it in an email and send it my way.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today.

In every age there are good things that never change, and bad things that never change too.
entry.summary: Rather than chasing trends and theories, the author believes the most meaningful work comes from understanding timeless human feelings and needs that have remained constant throughout history, regardless of era.

entry.title: A recommendation for chiirin (Chiikawa calligraphy practice)
entry.content:
I haven't gone in all that deep, but I'm having fun with it. Day after day, all I ever think about is "AI and Chiikawa." It's not that I've become some fanatic, but I keep at it. The day before yesterday, I started what I call "chiirin" (Chiikawa transcription practice). You know how everyone assumes that "Chiikawa" is just one of those "small and cute" things that seem to be everywhere?

Well, I thought so too, but I was completely wrong. For starters, if someone asked you, "Mom, try drawing one," could you actually draw one of those seemingly commonplace "Chiikawa" pictures? Sure, you could draw something similar, but you probably wouldn't get it right. What you'd end up with is something that bears no resemblance at all, something distinctly "un-Chiikawa-cute."

In other words, the way the creator, Nagano-sensei, draws "Chiikawa" is incredibly difficult. It's the mark of a true master, a work of consummate skill. I had a hunch this might be the case, so I tried copying one while looking at the original, and honestly, I just couldn't do it. It never came out looking good.

So I hit upon the idea of doing what the boss of my household does with calligraphy, which is to practice by transcribing a masterwork of the brush. For those "Chiikawa" pictures to exist on the page, there had to have been an "action," a specific movement of the brush, that gave rise to each of those lines. To transcribe a piece of calligraphy is to study the finished work closely and then reproduce, in my own hand, the "action" that once brought it into being. Copying a piece of writing is really about reproducing the act itself.

While turning over these knotty thoughts in my mind, I sit and draw the characters from "Chiikawa." The hardest parts are the outlines and the eyes. I can see exactly what the eyes are supposed to look like, but I just can't reproduce them. The position, the size, the thickness of the line, the tilt of each circular eye, all of it is the handiwork of a master. But then again, to learn is to imitate.

I believe that if I keep up my transcription practice every day, like copying out a sutra, I'll surely arrive at a state of "Chiikawa mastery, effortless and free." I really do recommend it, this daily "chiirin" (Chiikawa transcription practice).

◆And now, today's question. No. 017: "Are you stylish?" This one might be hard to answer, but let's give it some thought anyway. If you'd like, please write your answer in an email and send it my way.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. "Chiikawa transcription practice" costs almost nothing in materials or time, you know.
entry.summary: The author discovers that Chiikawa's seemingly simple aesthetic actually requires tremendous skill to recreate, and begins practicing daily transcription of the character's drawings as a form of meditative learning that mimics traditional calligraphy study.

entry.title: My own secret theory. But it's wrong.
entry.content:
There's an idea I keep to myself, one I'd never recommend to anyone else, but that I nonetheless "use." The idea is wrong. I know that. And one of these ideas is my theory of "fifty-fifty odds."

When you roll a die, hoping for a particular number, the chance of it coming up is one in six. Roll two dice and things get a little more complicated: seven has six ways of appearing, making it the most likely, while two and twelve each have only one way, so their odds are low. And yet, if there's a number I'm hoping for, say "three," then the outcome is simply this: either "three" comes up, or it doesn't.

It either appears or it doesn't, one of two possibilities, and so I decide, all on my own, that this makes it "fifty-fifty odds." You can see that this "theory (?)" is mistaken. Even so, as I rattle the dice in my hand, right up until the moment I let them go, I chant to myself: "fifty-fifty." Sometimes I miss. Sometimes I hit.

And this way of thinking, I actually "use" it (quietly, privately) in situations well beyond rolling dice. There's a kind of randomness, a not-knowing, much like a roll of the dice, that turns up in all sorts of moments in life. When that happens, quite apart from the version of me that's talking things over with everyone, I try to see the outcome as one of two things: either "it hits" or "it doesn't."

If it hits, I move on to whatever comes next. If it misses, I think about what to do next anyway. So either way, nothing ends right there on the spot. It becomes "Okay. On to the next one." What scares me more than anything is losing heart somewhere in that process. Eventually, the "three" or the "four" I was hoping for does come up.

In the truly important moments, I don't actually say any of this out loud. This isn't a matter of science. It's a matter of how you hold your heart.

◆ Today it's no.016: "How much do you walk in a day?" Steps are fine, distance is fine too. Try to recall. If you feel like it, jot it down in an email and send it my way.

Thank you, as always, for stopping by Hobonichi today.

For your daily record, there's the Hobonichi Techo and the Hobonichi Techo app.
entry.summary: The author describes a personal, flawed mental strategy of viewing uncertain life outcomes as simple fifty-fifty propositions, which helps them maintain resilience and forward momentum rather than losing heart when things don't go as hoped.

entry.title: What Chiikawa taught me.
entry.content:
These days I think about nothing but "AI" and "Chiikawa." Well, what can you do. They're worth thinking about, and what I think about is mine to decide, so I'll keep on thinking about "AI" and "Chiikawa." This too is what it means to value the "subjective."

When my daughter's daughter said, "I want to watch Chiikawa one more time," I asked her, "Shall we go watch it together with Shige-chan?" She fell silent, her face gone blank, as if all the warmth had drained out of it. Later she told me, in words I'd never heard from her before, "I didn't know what I was supposed to say." Ah, so it was something you'd never experienced or even thought about. I see.

Under the influence of Chiikawa (that is, of its creator, Nagano-san), I microwaved some frozen rice and ate it with butter and soy sauce. I've long known how good this is, but somehow it always got looked at as "the kind of thing a weirdo does," so ever since I entered the working world, I'd held myself back quite a bit. Natto is allowed, eggs are allowed, but butter is off-limits? I felt that way, and yet I never did it.

But thanks to my own personal "Chiikawa movement," I did it, and with a clear conscience too. It's delicious, of course. In the same spirit, I ordered some Myojo Charumera noodles. Both of these are things that, within the value system of adulthood, become the choice you make while thinking, "Well, this'll do."

But Nagano-sensei, and the Chiikawa characters too, truly eat these things saying, "This is delicious." The way it's depicted is so natural, so contented, so cool. Stronger than the mock-critic games of some gourmet blowhard, all lecture and "that stuff's no good," is a simple "This is delicious."

I think I can go back to being someone who eats butter-soy-sauce rice and Charumera with genuine relish. I won't get all preachy and quote proverbs like "I learn only to be content with what I have." No, it's just "This is delicious."

◆Now then, today's is no.015, "What would you do with 500 million yen?" This one might be surprisingly difficult. Please answer freely, from your own subjective view. If you'd like, write it out and send it to us by email.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. (I first wrote 100 million yen, then revised it up to 500 million. Ha.)
entry.summary: The essay celebrates how Chiikawa's simple, honest contentment with life's modest pleasures has freed the author from adult pretense, allowing them to unapologetically enjoy things like butter-soy-sauce rice that they'd previously dismissed as uncouth. Through this "Chiikawa movement," the author reclaims the genuine pleasure of saying "this is delicious" without irony or self-consciousness.

entry.title: Is a world full of optimal solutions really okay?
entry.content:
When you're about to start something, when you first begin turning it over in your mind, even if you have "no idea where to begin," I think that's actually pretty normal. You fumble around, this isn't it, that isn't it, what do I do? Was there a hint somewhere? Now I've lost the thread entirely... That's the kind of thing everyone has always done.

If it's a problem with a clear answer, someone practiced at solving them can rattle it off, sure. But most of the things we mull over in this world have answers that are vague at best. More than that, often we can't even properly make out what the problem is.

And yet, these days, if you just ask an "AI," it'll whip up the "optimal solution" for you in no time.

Someone I know, a person quite at home in life abroad, apparently traveled to a foreign country for the first time over the summer holidays. Up until now, the way they'd do it was this: for that first night's restaurant, you'd ask the guidebook or the hotel and have a safe, reliable meal. Then the next day you'd wander through the streets and happen to duck into some little place where the locals were lining up. That was the sort of rhythm of it.

But now, apparently, you can't help asking the "AI." The moment you arrive, it'll tell you about the kind of place "where the locals line up," the sort of spot you'd normally only stumble onto by luck. Delicious, pleasant, a flawless "optimal solution."

And this is wonderful, of course it is, it was a good thing. But still, they said, a thought crossed their mind.

If you keep chasing after these "optimal solutions" that the "AI" hands you, one after another, aren't you turning into "a person who's just following instructions"? A human being becomes an "automatic device" that "processes" "optimal solutions." Honestly, I get the feeling we're already halfway there.

Isn't there supposed to be more to living than that? Even if the "optimal solution" really is the optimal answer.

◆Today is no.014, "Is there a song you love?" Whether there is one or not, it's fine even just to pause and think, now that you mention it. And if you feel like it, write it in an email and send it our way.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today.

The fact that "I did it because I wanted to" is becoming something precious.
entry.summary: As AI increasingly provides perfect "optimal solutions" to our problems, we risk becoming passive followers of instructions rather than active participants in our own lives, losing the meaningful struggle and serendipity that make human experience valuable. The essay suggests that the quality of living lies not in achieving the best outcome, but in the genuine desire and personal agency we exercise in the process.

entry.title: A cry from the heart: "Don't underestimate me!"
entry.content:
The way I put this could rub people the wrong way, so I have to choose my words carefully. From something as vast as a nation or a cultural sphere, down to the grouchy old man next door or some random young guy on the street, the demand of "Don't underestimate me!" might just be, when you get right down to it, stronger, deeper, and more fierce than any other desire we carry.

If you take whatever people are arguing for in a quarrel or a moment of anger and boil it down to its very essence, it comes out as "Don't underestimate me!" Whether it's a sweeping historical epic, a domestic family drama, a war film, or a superhero story, what runs beneath any situation involving conflict is, more or less, this same theme.

The cry of "Don't underestimate me!" gets generally filed under words like "pride" or "self-respect," but it's not something you can tidy away into a noun like that. "Don't underestimate me!" isn't a concept, it's the cry of raw emotion. It can't be reasoned out in terms of gain and loss, and no amount of "because it's the right thing" will make it sit quietly.

To force others to acknowledge that "Don't underestimate me!", a person will seemingly do anything, without even sparing their own life. To make that feeling of "Don't underestimate me!" into something genuine, people work hard, endure, and pour out their blood and sweat. In a certain sense, they'll even steel themselves to be underestimated. So yes, there's actually good that comes out of "Don't underestimate me!" too.

But here's the thing. If you loosen the screws on that "Don't underestimate me!" signboard, just a little at a time, what you get in return, oddly enough, is "freedom." Between not being underestimated and being free, if you ask which is better, I'd say it's probably the latter. Though that part, I suppose, comes down to how each person chooses to live.

◆no.013: "Tell me anything at all about a book you've read." Today's Interview With You asks you this. Remember, reflect, and have a conversation with yourself. And if you'd like, write it in an email and send it my way.

Thank you for coming to Hobonichi today, too.

"It's nothing special," you say, but that's actually pretty special, you know.
entry.summary: The essay argues that the fundamental human desire to not be underestimated drives much of human conflict and motivation, yet paradoxically, releasing this need for recognition can lead to greater freedom and authenticity.

entry.title: I couldn't have done it on my own, but.
entry.content:
You tag along with a parent and end up experiencing something. It can be anything, really. Fishing, traveling, cooking, working the fields, digging a hole in the ground. Whatever it is, it becomes an experience. It's not something a child could do alone, but through it you learn, "Ah, so this is something that can be done." Just having done it once broadens your sense of what's possible, gives you the feeling that "this isn't beyond me."

I must have been not quite twenty at the time. My father, born in the eighth year of the Taisho era, rode on an airplane for the very first time. He seemed genuinely moved, thinking, "Now this is really something." So he told me to go and ride a plane too. He'd cover the cost, he said, so I should fly somewhere, anywhere. I suspect the idea of actually arranging it all himself and putting me on the plane felt too daunting, so he didn't want to go that far.

As for me, I was a provincial high school student in the 1960s who had never even set foot in an airport. Buying my own boarding pass and getting on a plane was something I simply didn't imagine I could do. It just wasn't in my world. And so my father's "go ride a plane" quietly faded away and came to nothing.

Children alive today must be different. Most of them have probably flown before, and the adults around them have all flown too, so they already know that getting on a plane "isn't beyond them." That difference, I think, is a fairly significant one.

My father, I imagine, had few experiences of doing something, of managing something, with the help of another person. It was a different era, and he hadn't been raised in wealth. So the world of things he could picture himself doing, the realm of "ah, so this can be done," was probably quite small. And I, raised by that father, followed his example. I had a strong streak of "I'll figure it out on my own."

The things you experience with the help of a parent or someone else get stored away in your memory as "things I'll probably be able to do myself someday." Looking back on my own life, I find that rather enviable. Doing everything from scratch, with nothing but your own two hands, isn't something you should choose on purpose.

◆Question no. 012: "Who did you rely on?" Any angle you approach it from is fine. Jot down your answer. And if you're willing, write it in an email and send it my way.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. "I've done that before" really does stay with you, doesn't it.
entry.summary: Shared experiences with parents—even simple ones—expand a child's sense of what's possible, creating a foundation of confidence that solitary achievement alone cannot provide.

entry.title: Because there should be plenty of "subjectivity," too.
entry.content:
I suspect that, for a while now, I'll be thinking and writing more and more about this one thing. It's the matter of "subjectivity."

Every day lately, as an ongoing series of "interviews with readers," I've been tossing out all sorts of questions. What I'm asking about always has something to do with that person's own subjective experience.

Well, to give an example: once I finish writing this piece today, I'll ask, "When was the last time you said goodbye?" Everyone, I imagine, says goodbye quite casually. An answer like "Oh, I just said it to so-and-so a moment ago" is perfectly fine. Some people might recall, "Come to think of it, I rarely go out of my way to actually say goodbye." And there may be someone who thinks, "It's not the goodbyes I've said that I remember, but the ones said to me." In other words, you picture something that actually happened to you.

And then, when you're specifically asked about it, you wonder which one to answer with, or you think, this one came to mind but I'll keep it to myself. You take something only you know, weigh it for yourself, and write it down for your own sake, or send it off in an email. There's no correct answer, it isn't a survey. You just think about what you thought, and jot it down. What lies at the root of it all is the memory of the life you've lived.

It's simple. Anyone who tries can do it, shallowly or deeply as they like. Slipping away from the question entirely is your own prerogative too. All you have to do is think and write, just as your subjectivity leads you.

But this is something "AI" cannot do. On the level of text, it may go through the exchange of saying "goodbye," but it's only saying it in a scene where "goodbye" is called for. It doesn't say goodbye because it wants to say goodbye. It's reproducing the form in which humans do these things.

As the situations where subjectivity is hard to voice keep multiplying, subjectivity turns to mist and slips out of sight. I want us to hold on more firmly to the fact that subjectivity exists. You, the person you are, are a you who possesses a subjectivity belonging to no one else.

◆So, yes. It's no. 011, "When was the last time you said goodbye?" Shall we take even just five minutes to remember, and give it some thought? If you'd like, please write it in an email and send it my way.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today.

Professor Ikujiro Nonaka once said that what you write in the Hobonichi Techo is your subjectivity.
entry.summary: The essay argues that subjectivity—our unique personal experiences and inner thoughts—is fundamentally human and irreplaceable, something AI can only imitate through form rather than genuine experience, and calls readers to actively preserve and articulate their own subjectivity through reflection and writing.

entry.title: Is it okay to just be vaguely happy?
entry.content:
I've been thinking about how to spend what people call the "Obon holiday," and I've come to a certain place. Both my wife and I have lost our parents, so neither of us has a family home to return to anymore. In a sense, I'm the family home now. People like us are free to spend Obon wherever we please. Then again, there's no need to make such a grand thing of it.

There's that expression, "this town is my second home," and it occurred to me how fortunate it would be to actually have such a place. And when I came here, I realized, ah, it isn't as though I don't have one. It's not that there's anything special here (which is a rude way to put it), but something about it, it just puts me at ease. There's no sightseeing to speak of. I move about a little, eat a meal at that one restaurant, catch sight of that one person's face, and that's about it.

The inn has a hot spring, so of course I'll be soaking in it. We arrived, greeted the people who invited us, shared a meal, and already I'm content. There's nothing else I need to do. Tomorrow there's a little "tourist spot" we'll drop by, but it's nothing to get worked up over. If it turns out nice, well, that's nice, and that's all there is to it.

We're here with my daughter's family, which of course means my daughter's daughter is here too. Ever since we were on the bullet train, I'd been sneaking glances at my granddaughter in the seat behind us, thoroughly enjoying myself. It was a bit like watching Panchan at the Ichikawa zoo. Just observing her is entertaining in itself. Forgive me, sweetheart, you're already thinking all sorts of grown-up thoughts, and here I am treating you like a child, comparing you to a little monkey.

Naturally, the conversation turns to "Chiikawa" as well. Of everyone gathered here, the two who know it best are this seven-year-old girl and me, at seventy-seven. Across a seventy-year gap in age, a proper Chiikawa discussion takes place. How good it is that this movie came out during the summer holidays. And how good it is that this town, my "second home," exists.

◆ There's no right answer, and the time spent thinking it over becomes a precious memory in itself. This is no.010, "What are your memories of your father?" Whether he's still here or gone, whether you loved him or didn't, anything at all. If you feel like it, write it down and send it to us by email.

Thank you, as always, for stopping by Hobonichi today. I love Tokyo dearly, but one way or another, it really is far too cramped!
entry.summary: As parents age and pass away, the concept of "home" shifts from a place to return to into something we carry with us—found in the simple comfort of familiar towns, shared meals, and meaningful moments with loved ones across generations.

entry.title: I want to make life easier for everyone.
entry.content:
Even without deliberately deciding to live, we go on living quite naturally, don't we. And along the way, we naturally do things that make life "easier to live." Eating, for instance, makes life easier to live for us. If we didn't eat, life would become harder to live. The same goes for sleeping, or relieving ourselves. These are all important things we do to make ourselves "easier to live." And building an environment where we can reliably do such things, that too is a way of making life "easier to live."

Some people might think there's a bare minimum of this and that which is all you need in order to live. But in reality, even when the bare minimum is in place, life doesn't become "easier to live." Simply having the conditions met means you can "live," yes, but it doesn't make life any easier to live. After all, someone serving a sentence in a prison facility has their "living" guaranteed too, don't they. And yet, that alone is precisely what makes it a "punishment."

Being able to use convenient things makes life easier to live. Having money makes life easier to live. Hurting others makes life harder to live. Deceiving others makes life harder to live. Being kind to others makes life easier to live.

What is it that makes life easier to live, and what makes it harder to live? Sometimes something makes life harder to live for a while, and yet eventually it's the very thing that makes life easier to live. Perhaps all of us, day by day, are living our lives working our hardest to make them "easier to live."

◆On another note, here is today's question for you. No. 009: "What temperature do you like the room to be?" Answer however you please. Jot it down in your planner, and if you like, write it in an email and send it to us as well.

Thank you for coming to Hobonichi today too. Starting today, I'm off on a summer trip. Just three days or so, mind you.
entry.summary: Life becomes truly livable not through meeting bare survival needs, but through access to comfort, kindness, and the things that ease our daily existence—a distinction between merely surviving and actually living well. The essay suggests we all instinctively strive each day to make life incrementally easier for ourselves and others, even if some struggles ultimately serve that same purpose.

entry.title: Looking back on 10 years, how was it?
entry.content:
People used to say, "Ten years makes an age." I think it was meant to convey something like, "Once ten years have passed, it's already the distant past." That if you're still carrying the same feelings you had ten years ago, well, you're already behind the times.

And I often found there was a lot of truth in it. Setting childhood aside, ten years as an adult feels short. I'll find myself recalling something from five or six years ago as though it were just the other day. And yet, once ten years have gone by, all sorts of things have changed. That, I think, was the pace at which the times moved. It's only a vague sense, but we used to mark off the years in tens, dividing up the eras that way.

But in the IT world, ten years was far more than "an age." It moved at a speed where the word "dog years" felt entirely natural. Yes, and just as a dog of ten is well into its "senior" years, perhaps the information society is already a "senior" itself, grown old.

And when it comes to everything outside the world of information, ten years ago, twenty years ago, thirty years ago, it all looks like more or less the same era carrying on. Whether or not you want to call that "stagnation," I really don't mind either way. The bullet trains got a little faster, the department stores gave way to sprawling electronics chains, people stopped carrying cash around, and yet nothing much really changed. And as things stand, there's no one out there to speak of a ten-years-from-now that young people might actually feel hopeful about.

Once you've followed all this and thought, "Yes, that's exactly how it is," the question becomes what each of us, each of our own "we," actually wants to do. What we "like." What we think is "good." Asking ourselves, and each other, all over again, that's what feels so terribly important to me right now.

◆ No. 008: "Tell me about something from ten years ago." Thank you for thinking about it each day. Treasure that time. You could jot it down in your notebook, a secret for no one else to see. And if you feel like it, please write it in an email and send it my way.

Thank you for coming to Hobonichi again today. As for my own past ten years, more than anything, I suppose it's that my daughter had a daughter of her own.
entry.summary: While technological progress has accelerated dramatically over the past decade, the non-digital world has stagnated, leaving us without a hopeful vision for the future—and thus forced to reckon with what we individually value and desire. The essay suggests that in times of uncertainty, rediscovering our own authentic preferences and connecting with others about them becomes essential.

entry.title: "Chiikawa" has few words but tons of facial expression.
entry.content:
As always, I've been thinking of nothing but "Chiikawa." The news keeps reporting that box office receipts have blown past 6.7 billion yen, that it's a massive hit, but surely all of that was simply "as expected." Because even with this many people pouring into theaters, there were still enough of the little bonus gifts to go around. Naturally, this is because each cinema had them ready and waiting. Those admission bonuses, the kind people say they'd "gladly pay money for," were manufactured in advance, more than a million of them, delivered to every theater in cardboard boxes and the like, and so they could be handed out. There was none of that frantic, scrambling chaos. If "Chiikawa" were a sports team, I'd find myself admiring what a formidable "defense" it has.

As for the film itself, people are offering their "interpretations" all over the place, so I'll hold back a little on that front.

Why is it that people want to talk about "Chiikawa" so very much? There are all sorts of reasons behind that secret, and I'm sure everyone wants to speak about those too, but the thing I find fascinating is this.

The main characters in "Chiikawa" hardly speak any actual "language" at all. The protagonist, Chiikawa, only ever manages little breathy exhales or small hesitant murmurs, and Usagi does nothing but let out these rallying yelps and nonsense cries, more like a toddler than anything. It's practically Hachiware alone who does the talking in real words. And the fact that that entire world holds together this way leaves the reader "room to imagine an enormous amount of language." Scenes where the characters simply nod at one another, or laugh together, come up again and again, and it just feels right. If the main characters put everything into words, there'd be no need for the reader to pour their own language into the gaps.

◆Today is no. 007: "What is the angriest you've ever been?" Whether from your past or your present, give it some thought and write it in your notebook. And if you'd like, please write it in an email and send it my way too.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. Even in my own circles, the number of "people who've seen Chiikawa" is multiplying at an accelerating pace.
entry.summary: The essay argues that "Chiikawa's" massive popularity stems from its minimal dialogue—the characters mostly communicate through sounds and gestures rather than words—which leaves readers and viewers abundant space to project their own interpretations and emotions onto the story.

entry.title: Things like "I like it" or "I love it."
entry.content:
When humans set out to make machines do something, the direction of progress has always been the same. Faster, stronger, more efficient, more abundant. This is easy to grasp, and easy to express in numbers. Look how much faster it's become, how much stronger, how much more it can do. "Fast, strong, efficient, abundant" can be compared, in a sense, by anyone, using numbers and the like.

And this kept developing, reaching a level the human eye can no longer see, no longer keep up with. What's more, this kind of evolution wasn't limited to the physical. It extended into the realm of what the brain does, too. From the era when we called them electronic calculators all the way to today's "generative AI," there has been an evolution almost violent in its intensity.

But that progress is centered on what can be compared through numbers and symbols, on what anyone can clearly evaluate. If "fast, strong, efficient, abundant" were the sole standard for all "value" in the world, there would be no room for any complicated judgment. Everything would be neatly settled by this alone.

And yet the human being, the "agent" that sets the things of this world in motion, makes judgments by a rather different set of values, chooses accordingly, and sometimes even stakes his life on that choice. "Good," "beautiful," "interesting," "adorable," "drawn to it." These are values that can't be compared in numbers or symbols, that resist even being defined, and in the actual world they are always being asked about, actively, restlessly.

No matter how hard you try to "put it into words (into symbols)," the most you can do is trace a faint outline around the value. It stays in the realm of "I don't really get it, but it's just so wonderful!"

We used to name this kind of "value" art and fence it off separately, but it also belongs to the territory of "chic" and "cool." I don't understand it, but things are getting interesting around here!

◆An interview with you again today. No. 006: "What was the first lie you ever told, and the last one?" Jot it down, and if you feel like it, write it in an email and send it to us.

Thank you for coming to Hobonichi today, too.

We cherish what human beings feel, sense, and think.
entry.summary: While machines progress measurably through speed and efficiency, human value ultimately derives from ineffable qualities like beauty, charm, and meaning that resist quantification and remain fundamentally mysterious. The essay argues that these intangible human judgments—the "wonderful" that can't be put into words—are as essential to how we navigate the world as the numerical progress we celebrate.

entry.title: Keep saying that and you'll get stalked.
entry.content:
Hot again today, isn't it. But you know, no matter how much you complain about the heat, it doesn't make the heat go away. All that muttering about how hot it is just fixes your mind on it, and then you can't stop thinking about the heat all day long. You spend your whole day haunted by the spirit that lives inside those words. And whoever happens to be nearby gets dragged into it too, chased around by "it's so hot, it's so hot" for no fault of their own.

It's the same with everything, really. There are people who do nothing but grumble that they've got no money. And it's never the ones who actually have none, it's the ones who just love to say it. Does the money rain down from heaven because you keep saying you haven't got any? Is somebody going to hand you cash just because you claim to be broke? If a fellow opens his mouth only to say he's skint, skint, skint, then folks around him figure they'll never see their money again if they lend it, and they clam up their wallets. This sort of thing pulls other people in too, so you really ought to watch yourself.

Unpleasant things, worries, there's no end of them. Even when it looks like you've got none, go looking and you'll find some. And what pleasure is there in dredging that stuff up over and over, making other people sigh? Well, I suppose they do it because they like doing it. "Even the heat gets forgiven only three times," same as the patience of a saint, and that's about right.

That's the sort of thing I meant to write, but whenever I set it down the usual way I end up holding back and softening it. So today I channeled the spirit of the master storyteller Tatekawa Danshi and spoke through him.

Now then, a little more about the "100 Questions Interview." I'm grateful for it, because people share what they've been thinking, and it makes me feel as though I'm meeting and talking with lots of people every day.

◆Today's is no. 005, "Can you swim?" Nice and simple. It's summer, after all, so have some fun with this one. Jot your thoughts and feelings down in your notebook and let them accumulate. And if you feel like it, write them in an email and send them my way.

Thank you for coming to Hobonichi again today. As for me, I went to the movies at night and watched "Chiikawa" for the third time.
entry.summary: Complaining about problems—whether heat, money troubles, or worries—only fixes your mind on them and drags others down with you, so it's better to simply avoid dwelling on and voicing unpleasant things. The author uses this insight to encourage readers to focus their energy on more positive activities, like responding to the "100 Questions Interview" about simple topics like swimming.

entry.title: More about the "100 questions interview"
entry.content:
We've only just started, but this "Interview of 100 Questions," the one I'm putting to those of you reading this, is turning out to be quite fascinating.

I began it in a light spirit, thinking of it as a kind of "daily bonus," but it might just become something deeper than that. Over a hundred days, the accumulated thoughts of a fair number of people could amount to something like "a memory of an era, and of human beings." Perhaps no one has ever attempted, or recorded, anything quite like it before.

These days, you're always being pressed to answer right away, aren't you? "Which is it?" Left or right, friend or foe, like it or hate it, answer now. But this is nothing like that. There's no correct answer, no objective, no survey being conducted. It's simply time spent by a great many people "thinking about something." That's what I proposed we record.

Honestly, it's perfectly fine if you forget what you thought afterward. I did say to write in and tell me by email, but there's no better or worse, no skilled or clumsy here. "Everyone's is good." I just felt that if, here and there, the questions became a chance for people to pause for a moment and "ask themselves something," then that would be enough.

Because think about it, take a question like "What's your favorite flower?" Unless someone asks you outright, you rarely stop to consider it, right? By asking yourself and "turning it over in your mind," you end up discovering yourself anew: "Oh, so I'm someone who loves camellias." That sort of thing.

The truth is, I'm thinking through my own answers too, even as I'm the one asking. Someday I may reveal them, but I also feel it's my own freedom to keep some of them to myself forever.

In that sense, I don't think you should treat your answers as something "for the email." Sometimes you can keep a secret a secret, and simply write it down in a notebook that belongs to you alone.

◆Now then, let's carry on with today's interview.

No. 004: "What sort of place do you live in?"

First, think about it freely, and jot it down. And if you feel like it, write it in an email and send it my way.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. If we keep this up for a hundred rounds, I'm sure "your very own book" will take shape.
entry.summary: This essay celebrates a unique hundred-question interview project designed not to survey or judge, but to encourage people to pause and reflect on themselves through thoughtful consideration of seemingly simple questions. By creating space for genuine introspection without pressure or "correct" answers, the author believes the accumulated responses will form a meaningful collective memory of an era and human nature.

entry.title: I spent years overlooking "Chiikawa."
entry.content:
There's a phrase, "swing at the good ones," which Mister himself, Shigeo Nagashima, once brushed onto a signature board. Hit the good pitches without fail, leave the bad ones alone, and good results will follow. "Chiikawa," for instance, was one of those good pitches.

Right now I'm working my way not only through every volume of "Chiikawa" but also through the manga the author drew before it, and I find myself impressed at every turn. Lately what's been quietly moving me is the way she handles "pauses" and "lingering resonance." The artist who draws it is wonderful, and I think the reader who gets to savor it is lucky too. This is something that always existed in Japanese four-panel and eight-panel manga, so it isn't as though it's some brand-new technique, but this "expression through what isn't drawn," akin to haiku or tanka, truly lands in the reader's heart with remarkable skill. If Ms. Itsuki Natsui, the haiku poet, were to read "Chiikawa," I bet she could discuss it as poetry.

But you know, here I am saying that "Chiikawa" and "AI" are all I think about these days, and yet until a few months ago this was a pitch I let sail right past me, dismissing it with a "yeah, I know it, so what?" Just a called strike. "Chiikawa" means "small and somehow cute," and because that almost seems to say it all, you just breeze past with "nice, kind of cute" and leave it at that.

Then one day I learned why the character "Momonga" plays up the cutesy act the way it does, and suddenly I was hooked, thinking, "wait, what is that all about?!" Come to think of it, Hobonichi's relationship with "Chiikawa" goes all the way back to the "Gentle Towel" in 2022, yet even then I was only looking at it thinking, "oh, that's nice, cute." My curiosity was fast asleep as I gazed at "Chiikawa." I hadn't taken my stance with any intention of swinging the bat (lesson learned).

◆Now, a question, no. 003: "What's your favorite way to play?" Think about it freely in your own way and jot it down in your notebook. And if you'd like, write it in an email and send it my way.

Thank you again today for coming to Hobonichi. Though there's a limit to how many pitches you can hit on personal curiosity alone.
entry.summary: The author reflects on how initially dismissing "Chiikawa" as merely cute caused her to miss its sophisticated use of artistic pauses and implied meaning—a reminder that truly appreciating worthwhile things requires genuine curiosity and engagement rather than casual surface-level judgment.

entry.title: Shigesato Itoi will continue interviews for 100 days.
entry.content:
On a bit of a whim, I've started something new: interviewing you, the reader. (Confusing, isn't it?) Yesterday was the very first installment, and I asked, "What kind of child were you?" Remember?

The idea is to take a fresh look at how you think about your own childhood. And then to jot it down in your notebook, so you won't forget. Your answer might change later on, and even if it does, well, that just means you gave it some more thought, so that's perfectly fine too.

Your own childhood is the sort of thing you might never stop to consider unless someone asks. But then again, maybe you have thought about it, just a little. It lives in that hazy, half-formed territory, doesn't it?

Since there are surely things people would rather not share with others, I wrote, "Feel free to email me if you'd like." And then I received quite a number of emails. Many people said things like, "Thank you for this wonderful opportunity," which honestly put me at ease and made me happy.

And here's the thing: it fascinated me how many people said, "I was a bit of a sly child." We tend to imagine children as pure and innocent, yet so many people admitted, "I was a bit of a cunning kid." I'd count myself among them, for that matter. That kind of slyness is something I'd like to take another look at.

I'm prepared to keep this interview going all the way to a hundred questions. My hunch is that as you answer them one by one, a version of "yourself" you thought you knew but didn't quite will start to come into view. I'll weave together the simple questions and the wildly unexpected ones. No matter what, I'm going to see all hundred through.

So, on to the momentous second question.

No. 002: "Is there someone more important to you than yourself?"

Whatever your answer turns out to be, be sure to record it in your notebook. And of course, if you'd like, please write it down and send it to me by email.

Thank you for coming to Hobonichi today, too. Lately, all I ever think about is "Chiikawa" and "AI."
entry.summary: The author launches a series of 100 self-reflective interview questions designed to help readers examine their own lives more deeply, starting with childhood memories and moving toward questions about values and relationships. Through the unexpectedly candid responses received, the author discovers that self-examination can reveal hidden truths about ourselves that we rarely pause to consider.

entry.title: Beyond the top of the vocal range. The darkness seen with closed eyes.
entry.content:
So, do you do karaoke, that sort of thing? Even if not karaoke, do you ever sing? When you sing, there's this thing called vocal range, and at some point, both on the low end and the high end, the notes just stop coming out. There are notes other people can hit that you simply can't. But what if you don't actually voice them, can you imagine higher and higher notes without limit? Just imagining seems like it should be possible, doesn't it? Shall we give it a try? This is something I thought up and tested back in my twenties. What I found was that as I went up an octave, and then another, at some point I was just cycling through the same range over and over without realizing it (I wrote about this on Hobonichi back in 1998, too). It turns out there's a limit even to the "imagination" of sound. When I first wrote about this, Yosuke Yamashita, the jazz musician, told me, "That was really interesting," and I remember being tremendously happy about it.

Now then, I recently discovered something along these same lines again. At night, in that stretch between getting into bed and drifting off to sleep, it's no good to let your mind wander to pointless things, so I decided that after closing my eyes I would picture some lovely scene and just gaze at it there behind my eyelids. But this "lovely scene" I wanted to gaze at turned out to be surprisingly hard to conjure up. After trying all sorts of things, lately I've settled on this baffling theme of "the dark reaches of outer space," and I've made that my thing to look at. Since it's basically just "darkness," it's fine for it to be vague. If I stare at it and things go well, I sink pleasantly into sleep.

And while doing this, at one point I realized something: I'm looking at this "darkness" with my dominant eye. I'm viewing the "darkness" mainly with my left eye, so what is my right eye doing? It's providing "support," you see, backing up the dominant eye. Now, I can look at the "darkness" with just my right eye too, but somehow that leaves me unsettled. And that's it. Today's story comes to its abrupt little end right here.

Now, from here on it's an interview with you. Jot it down somewhere, in a notebook (or a notebook app), and if you feel like it, go ahead and send it to me by email as well.

No. 001: "What kind of child were you growing up?"

Thank you for coming to Hobonichi today, too. This closing interview, I intend to keep it up every day until I get tired of it.
entry.summary: The essay explores how our perception has inherent limits—from the inability to imagine vocal notes beyond a certain range to the challenge of consciously visualizing pleasant scenes—revealing that even our imagination operates within physical and neurological constraints. Through personal observations about singing, sleep visualization, and eye dominance, the author discovers that our minds cannot infinitely extend sensory experiences the way we might theoretically expect them to.

entry.title: What does the real me like, and what do I want to do?
entry.content:
Some insects and animals, it seems, use tools. Nothing terribly elaborate, but they manage things their "born-and-raised-as-is" bodies couldn't do on their own, using a twig here, a torn-off leaf there. Monkeys don't make pottery or stone tools, but surely they'll pick something up off the ground and put it to use. Even that much is no small thing.

Human beings, on the other hand, live buried in tools. To move, to cook, to play, to make things, and beyond that, we even make tools for making tools. Add to that the ability to think using language, and we've come to feel as though there's nothing we can't do. Think it up, and you can build the very thing you thought of. That's astonishing. At this point, no monkey or crow could ever catch up to us.

And now that "generative AI" has entered the picture too, we're drifting into an age where we might forget what humans could even do in the first place.

But we mustn't forget, and I don't want to forget. Just how much can a person do with nothing but their own flesh and bone? We lean so completely on tools and machines to get through life, but how much can we really do with our own two hands? How far could we get by drawing on everything we've learned and everything we've done up to now? (Maybe that's the sort of thing they explore in sports.) What could we do if we couldn't borrow anyone else's help? What is it we would absolutely refuse to do? If there were something we wanted to protect no matter what, what would it be? And what are the things we truly love?

Normally nobody asks us these things, and there's no particular reason anyone would. But I think those questions, and their answers, and the process of thinking them through, are precisely what make up "me, and no one else."

Tools and machines have come to do everything for us, but "what do I want done?" and "how do I want to be?" are still things that "I, and no one else" get to decide.

Before I forget it all, I want to remember.

Thank you for coming to Hobonichi again today. Interviewing yourself might be something worth doing every single day.
entry.summary: As humans become increasingly dependent on tools and AI to accomplish everything, we risk forgetting what we can do with our own hands and minds—and more importantly, losing touch with the uniquely personal questions that define who we are. The essay urges us to regularly examine what we truly value and how we want to live, before we outsource these fundamental aspects of our humanity entirely.

entry.title: Sweet potato tempura with a firm batter.
entry.content:
When people praise tempura, they always say things like, "The batter is light and crisp." Crunchy, no hint of oiliness, light. That's what everyone reaches for. And I agree. I really do.

That said, the tempura you get at udon chains and places like that isn't light at all, and it certainly isn't crisp. If anything, the batter is thick enough to have opinions of its own, and rather than light, you'd have to call it hard.

But is that bad? Is it unpleasant? Not to me. I actually want this kind of tempura too. Especially the sweet potato ones. I'm fine with batter so hard it clunks against your teeth. And I'm certainly not going to talk about how it "doesn't taste of oil." I'll even go and pile on extra tempura crumbs.

They're both tempura, and they're both good, aren't they? No need to rush to declare that this one is proper and that one isn't. They're both delicious.

With just about anything, there's a kind of "accepted standard for what counts as good." Things that have been around a long time naturally develop one. Tempura, sushi, grilled fish, soba, udon, all of them come with a set of "words of praise" that everyone more or less knows.

But even if you know those words, I think it might be better to set them aside for a while. "Springy, chewy udon" is delicious, of course, but there's no reason we can't also discover the deliciousness of "soft, sloppy udon."

Being unhygienic or unclean is another matter, but I really do think that finding "deliciousness" from a different angle deserves to be valued more.

Come to think of it, the things people call "old-fashioned" include "firm pudding," "omelettes that aren't all soft and runny," and "salmon that's too salty," don't they? I'm sure there are plenty more if you go looking.

Right now, at two in the morning, I want a bowl of udon with hard tempura on top.

Thank you for coming to Hobonichi again today. Though honestly, the ordinary words of praise turn out to be right more often than not.
entry.summary: Rather than blindly following established standards for what makes food "good," we should embrace our own discovery of deliciousness in unexpected forms—whether that's hard tempura or soft udon—and value these unconventional pleasures alongside traditional ideals.

entry.title: Adults have "feelings" too.
entry.content:
"You only understand your parents' devotion once you have children of your own." Well, it really is true, isn't it. You could swap in all sorts of other positions and it would still hold. "You only understand your teacher's kindness once you have students," or "You only understand your senior's kindness once you have juniors." I've done a lot of things over a long time now, so all I can really say is, "Sorry, truly, for everything."

The ones who learn something first, who figure it out first, teach it and pass it on to the ones who come after. And the ones who come along later to learn it, well, they don't feel especially grateful. They just take the teaching for granted. It's probably something close to instinct. The monkeys up on Monkey Mountain do it, dogs and cats do it. And humans, too, keep repeating this same pattern, quite naturally.

Say "a parent's devotion" and it starts to sound like some moral lesson, but there's a gentler way to put it: "a parent's feelings." Why did my own parents do the things they did, say the things they said? Once you become a parent yourself, these things start to make sense.

During summer vacation in elementary school, we had radio calisthenics in the schoolyard. I imagine they still do it in places that still do it. I'd hang the little card around my neck, the one you got stamped each day, and head off, grumbling to myself about how much of a pain it was to get up so early. I'd just sort of drift over to the school with the other kids from the neighborhood.

Then one day, my father, who was always hungover and never a morning person, announced, "Radio calisthenics are good for your health, so I'm coming too," and off he went to the school with me. I was a little embarrassed to go with a parent, but there was also a tiny part of me that felt happy about it, and so the two of us walked together to Momoi Elementary for the morning exercises.

That's the whole memory, nothing more, but now I understand it. It wasn't really "because it's good for your health." He simply wanted to tag along and do the calisthenics with his elementary-school kid. If there was a chance to be with your child, you wanted to be with them. That was the feeling behind it, I now see. And I understand it because I'm the same way myself.

Thank you for coming to Hobonichi today. There's also the saying, "A parent's heart, unknown to the child," and I rather like that one too.
entry.summary: The essay reflects on how we only truly understand our parents' actions and sacrifices when we become parents ourselves, revealing that what seemed like simple duties or rules were actually expressions of love and a desire to be close to their children.

entry.title: The real problem you want to solve isn't that one.
entry.content:
Since this is something I've experienced myself, I can't really speak too harshly about it. But at a certain point in my life, I came to understand this: "When a person is caught up in something to an abnormal, almost obsessive degree, the thing they truly need to resolve is probably something else entirely."

The things a person really wants to resolve, I think, aren't all that many. Relationships close to home, like family or a lover. Social relationships tied to one's pride, like work not going well. Concrete financial troubles, like debt. These are the kinds of things that, if you seriously set out to deal with them, demand a considerable amount of resolve. Getting angry won't help. Grieving won't help. It's hard to find your way to a solution. And even if there's someone willing to lend a hand, the one who has to push through the pain and keep going is you.

"Being fanatically absorbed in something" is a state that radiates energy, and the sight of someone earnestly devoted to a task can look, somehow, like a deeply convincing way to live. So I completely understand throwing yourself into it. And because you're doing it so earnestly, so passionately, it becomes: "I don't have time for anything else."

This is exactly the point. That "anything else" is precisely where "the thing you truly wanted to resolve" was supposed to be all along.

At a certain point, I looked back on my own past self and understood, in hindsight, that this is how it works. The personal, "inner" problems you have to resolve yourself, you try to forget them by placing importance on "outer" problems instead. For lack of a better term, I've come to call this "the externalization of a problem."

Beyond the realm of comfort, entertainment, or play, people pour in their anger, their sorrow, even their health, and sink completely into it. Cases like this, I think, are only increasing in these times.

Thank you again for coming to Hobonichi today. Though I myself used to get called a "fanatical Giants fan."
entry.summary: The essay argues that obsessive absorption in external pursuits often masks unresolved personal problems—relationships, work, finances—that we unconsciously avoid by channeling our energy into something that feels productive but ultimately distracts us from what we truly need to face.

entry.title: The one cornering you might be yourself.
entry.content:
It's not really my place to say this, being the half-hearted coward that I am (and I've packed in more kanji than usual here), but I suspect that in a good many of the cases where we tell ourselves "there's no escape" or "I have no choice," escape is actually possible. It would probably be more persuasive if I went through concrete examples one by one, but that's a hassle, so I won't. And blithely saying "that's a hassle, so I won't" is itself a way of running from the trouble of taking the trouble.

Maybe, to get through to more people in a way they'd really understand, I ought to offer some real examples. But even as I think that might be true, I wonder: would doing so actually get the point across all that well?

Take the old saying, "even a dog that walks will bump into a stick." It isn't concrete communication in the slightest. Some people will think there's no use listening to a story about a dog. Others will want to say, "So what?" And yet that abstract, seemingly empty phrase can suddenly come back to a person and set them walking again.

Now, let me return to that first "there's no escape." If, in roughly the same offhand way as the dog and the stick, you happen to remember that some half-hearted coward once said, "situations you think you can't escape, that you have no choice about, are actually pretty escapable," it just might be that the memory comes alive and starts to move. I suppose I half believe in that, which is why I'm sitting here writing this meddlesome little piece.

You could shorten it to: "You can get out of things more easily than you'd think." I've said it before in another form, too: "People don't actually do the things they truly hate." Often enough, you're only tied down by ropes you've wrapped around yourself.

Today, some volunteers from Hobonichi are running through the scorching heat of Tokyo. They're carrying a delivery in a relay all the way to Tadanori Yokoo's place. "Make your peace with the heat," I offered, by way of encouragement.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. Freedom is something we go and sell off of our own accord.
entry.summary: Most of what we perceive as inescapable constraints are actually self-imposed, and remembering this simple truth—even in abstract or offhand form—can be enough to set us free.

entry.title: "Let's do what we can" still holds true today.
entry.content:
No matter what happens, the answer is always: "Let's do what we can." Emotions may hurry us along, may leave us unsettled, but eventually, the "things each of us can do" should slowly come into view. The help we need right away, the assistance required along the way, and the long, patient support. All of it is necessary, together with a feeling of prayer.

Well then, today too, I'll paste in yesterday's little scraps of notes.

Even though I own so many nail clippers, I've stepped down, for now, from that whole nail-clipper connoisseur game. Why? Because I've started using a glass nail file. Being able to care for your nails without any blade at all, it's really something. Come to think of it, some villainous boss in an old movie used a nail file too. So, heh, maybe I'm a villainous boss myself now...

I came up with my own eternal phrase. "There are all kinds of people. It can't be helped." I've genuinely come to feel this way. By "all kinds" I mean good and bad, right and wrong, every last bit of it. You can't dye all these different people into a single color, and you mustn't try. On top of accepting that, you team up, you give up, you find your separate spaces to live. Nature became the nature we know now precisely through this process.

Apparently a new series of "Shinya Shokudo" is starting again this autumn. It began in 2009, and it's been seven years since the last one. I love that the staff and cast are reuniting. Yesterday, Kaoru Kobayashi came by Hobonichi and talked with us about "Shinya Shokudo," complete with plenty of idle chatter.

That feeling of "I want to work with that team" has grown much larger for me than all sorts of other conditions. I heard that an amazing crew has gathered for the "Chiikawa" film, and what that means is, it became a team where the doers show up, the ones thinking "I want to work alongside people like that." I think any kind of work heads in this direction. Thank you for coming to Hobonichi today, too. I'd like to think of the blisteringly hot days and the merely somewhat hot days as two separate things.
entry.summary: Rather than seeking perfect solutions, the essay advocates for doing what we can with acceptance and collaboration—whether caring for our nails with gentleness, embracing human diversity without judgment, or choosing to work with people we genuinely want to team up with. The key insight is that progress comes not from forcing uniformity or perfection, but from patient, collective effort guided by realistic compassion.
